question.prompt: How many ways are there to split the integers \(1\) through \(14\) into \(7\) pairs such that in each pair, the greater number is at least \(2\) times the lesser number?

solutions.explanation:
Choose partners for the most restricted numbers first. This will let us count the choices at each step without splitting into many cases.

First, which numbers can be the smaller members of their pairs? A smaller member cannot be \(8\) or more: its partner would have to be at least \(16\), which is unavailable. Each of the seven pairs contributes a different smaller member. Since all seven smaller members lie among \(1,2,\ldots,7\), they must use every number in that set. Their larger partners must therefore be \(8,9,\ldots,14\).

Now \(7\) can only partner \(14\). This is why choosing freely for \(1\) first would be awkward: using \(14\) would take the only possible partner for \(7\). Work downward from \(7\) instead.

Pair \(7\) with \(14\): one choice. The partner of \(6\) must be at least \(12\). With \(14\) used, either \(12\) or \(13\) works: two choices.

The partner of \(5\) must come from \(10,11,12,13,14\). Both earlier partners lie in this five-number set, so exactly two eligible numbers have been used. That leaves three choices, whichever partner we chose for \(6\).

Any of \(8,9,\ldots,14\) is large enough to partner \(4\), and three have been used, leaving four choices. After that, three larger numbers remain. All are large enough to partner \(3\), so it has three choices. Then \(2\) has two choices, and \(1\) takes the last number.

The number of choices at each step stays the same regardless of the earlier choices. The multiplication principle therefore gives

\[
1\cdot2\cdot3\cdot4\cdot3\cdot2\cdot1=\boxed{144}.
\]

Each pairing is counted once: the fixed order \(7,6,\ldots,1\) tells us exactly when to choose each pair. The answer is E.

When partner restrictions become tighter for larger numbers, try handling those numbers first. The useful check before multiplying is that earlier choices always remove the same number of eligible partners.
solutions.title: Choose partners from the most restricted number downward.
